summary: Psalm 141 is a short plea for urgent help, disciplined speech, and protection from joining the ways of the wicked. The speaker asks that prayer be received like incense, welcomes correction from the righteous, describes severe danger, and ends by asking to pass safely while the wicked fall into their own traps.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows Book V of Psalms still making room for distress, moral danger, and unresolved threat. It teaches readers to notice how a prayer can ask both for rescue from enemies and for guarding from becoming like them.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David,” but Psalms’ Davidic headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; their exact force is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later received by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private use.
context.date: The individual psalms come from different periods, and the final five-book Psalter is a later anthology; this chapter cannot be dated precisely from its wording and heading alone.
context.setting: The speaker is under pressure from wicked people and asks Yahweh for help, guarded speech, correction, and refuge.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, using compressed images such as incense, a door, oil on the head, scattered bones, snares, traps, and nets.

outline.heading: Urgent prayer rising before Yahweh
outline.note: The speaker calls on Yahweh to come quickly and asks that prayer be accepted like incense and lifted hands like the evening sacrifice.

outline.heading: Guarded speech and guarded desire
outline.note: The prayer turns inward, asking Yahweh to watch the mouth, keep the lips, and prevent the heart from being drawn into evil deeds or the delicacies of the wicked.

outline.heading: Correction welcomed, evil opposed
outline.note: The speaker says correction from the righteous is kindness, while continuing to pray against evil deeds.

outline.heading: Judges cast down and bones scattered
outline.note: The psalm describes the downfall of judges and a vivid image of bones scattered at the mouth of Sheol.

outline.heading: Refuge from snares and nets
outline.note: The speaker fixes his eyes on Yahweh, asks not to be left destitute, and prays to escape the traps laid by workers of iniquity while the wicked fall into their own nets.

keyVerses.text: Let my prayer be set before you like incense; the lifting up of my hands like the evening sacrifice.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the psalm’s worship language, comparing prayer and raised hands to recognized temple images without explaining the ritual in detail.

keyVerses.text: Set a watch, Yahweh, before my mouth. Keep the door of my lips.
keyVerses.why: The danger is not only outside the speaker; the psalm asks for protection over speech itself.

keyVerses.text: Let the righteous strike me, it is kindness; let him reprove me, it is like oil on the head; don’t let my head refuse it; Yet my prayer is always against evil deeds.
keyVerses.why: This verse shows the speaker wanting correction from the righteous while resisting evil deeds.

keyVerses.text: For my eyes are on you, Yahweh, the Lord. I take refuge in you. Don’t leave my soul destitute.
keyVerses.why: The verse gathers the psalm’s trust: attention fixed on Yahweh, refuge sought, and abandonment feared.

themes: The wicked caught in their own nets

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading says, “A Psalm by David,” so the received text associates the poem with David. Readers differ on whether such headings normally name the author, mark association with a Davidic collection, or preserve mixed kinds of information. The body of the psalm presents an “I” who calls on Yahweh, asks for guarded speech, and seeks protection from the wicked.

questions.question: Why compare prayer to incense and the evening sacrifice?
questions.answer: Verse 2 uses worship images to ask that the speaker’s prayer be accepted before Yahweh. The psalm does not pause to explain the rituals; it simply places spoken prayer and lifted hands in relation to incense and the evening sacrifice.

questions.question: What does “Set a watch” mean here?
questions.answer: In verse 3, the speaker asks Yahweh to guard his mouth and lips as if they were an entry that needed watching. The image treats speech as a place of danger where harm can enter or leave.

questions.question: Is the speaker only asking to be protected from other people?
questions.answer: No. The psalm asks for rescue from snares and traps, but it also asks that the speaker’s own heart not be inclined toward evil and that his mouth be guarded. The danger is both external pressure and internal participation in wickedness.

questions.question: What are the “delicacies” in verse 4?
questions.answer: The word appears in the line, “Don’t let me eat of their delicacies.” In context, it belongs with practicing wicked deeds alongside “men who work iniquity.” The image suggests something attractive or desirable that would draw the speaker into their company, but the psalm does not identify a specific meal or event.

questions.question: Why would the speaker call being struck by the righteous “kindness”?
questions.answer: Verse 5 contrasts correction from the righteous with evil deeds. The speaker says reproof is like oil on the head and asks not to refuse it. The point is not that all striking is good, but that this prayer values correction that turns the speaker away from evil.

questions.question: What is happening in verses 6-7?
questions.answer: These are the hardest lines in the psalm. The text says “their judges are thrown down by the sides of the rock,” then gives an image of bones scattered “at the mouth of Sheol.” Interpreters debate the exact situation, but the verses clearly picture violent downfall and extreme vulnerability.

questions.question: What is Sheol?
questions.answer: In this verse, Sheol appears in the phrase “the mouth of Sheol,” beside the image of scattered bones. The psalm uses it as a place associated with death or the grave, without giving a full teaching about the afterlife.

questions.question: How does the psalm end?
questions.answer: It ends with a request for reversal. The speaker asks to be kept from the snare and traps laid by workers of iniquity, and then asks that the wicked fall into their own nets while he passes by. The psalm does not narrate the rescue; it leaves the request before Yahweh.

glossary.def: A fragrant offering image used in verse 2 to describe how the speaker wants his prayer to be set before Yahweh.
The worship image paired with lifted hands in verse 2.
Wrongdoing named in verses 4 and 9, connected with people whose deeds and traps threaten the speaker.
The term in verse 7 used in an image of death or the grave, “the mouth of Sheol.”
A trap image in verse 9 for the danger laid for the speaker.
